Header:

Summary:
Quick tech deep dive after Meridian flagged intermittent p99 spikes during peak auth flows. SE-led with AE present to capture next steps and commercial constraints.

[00:00] Samira Khan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, Samira from Redwood here. Diego's joining as well, he'll drive the perf bits. Clara, Ethan, you ok on time?
[00:06] Clara Li: Yep, can hear you. We have Ravi and Maya on as well, thanks for doing this.
[00:10] Diego Ruiz: Hi team. Quick agenda — symptoms, what we measured, possible root causes, then controlled experiments. Sound good?
[00:16] Ethan Brooks: Yep. We really want to understand whether it's network hops or KV caching hot spots. Our SLA calls for p99 < 350ms on short prompts, and we're seeing bursts to 800ms randomly.
[00:28] Ravi Patel: Those spikes look correlated with specific customer workloads but not all. We suspect some paths through our transit gateway add jitter.
[00:34] Diego Ruiz: Okay, helpful. Can you confirm whether you use streaming responses in prod or non-streaming?
[00:40] Maya Gomez: We switched to streaming for conversational flows — mostly token-by-token with gRPC streaming — but some batch jobs still use non-streaming full-response endpoints.
[00:49] Samira Khan: Good, that gives us a surface to compare. Streaming tends to surface network hop variance immediately — you see tail tokens delayed if one packet drops or a hop spikes, whereas non-streaming hides it until the end.
[00:58] Clara Li: Right, that's what we thought. But some of the spikes also happen on non-streaming calls, which is confusing.
[01:05] Diego Ruiz: Two likely mechanisms: A) network variance causing a straggler in a multi-hop path (Envoy sidecar or transit gateway) and B) KV cache hot shard — if the token prefix cache misses and we fetch from remote disk or a colder KV node, you get a big outlier for that request.
[01:22] Ravi Patel: We're using a mix of on-prem and VPC private: primary model hosting is Redwood Dedicated in us-east-1, and an on-prem fallback in our colo via VPC peering. Could cross-region peering be causing this?
[01:34] Diego Ruiz: Yes — cross-region or cross-AZ peering, plus asymmetric routing, can introduce additional hops. Also packet pacing from older NICs can create microbursts that look like tail events.
[01:46] Ethan Brooks: We saw one incident where p99 spiked during a GC window in an older on-prem node — maybe a kernel stall. How much of tail behavior is due to host jitter vs model runtime?
[01:55] Diego Ruiz: Both. On the runtime side, quantized kernels can be non-deterministic in latency depending on memory alignment and sharded GEMM scheduling, especially if you mix int8 kernels with fallback fp16 code paths. On host side, CPU interrupts, cgroup throttling, or noisy neighbors on the NIC matter.
[02:12] Clara Li: Do you have recommendations for quantization profiles that reduce variance?
[02:16] Diego Ruiz: In general, per-layer symmetric quantization with a static calibration profile reduces runtime branching. Also pinning threads and using isolated hugepages helps. But the biggest wins for tail are caching and routing: avoid cold KV cache misses for hot prefixes.
[02:31] Samira Khan: We shared a spreadsheet earlier comparing token throughput across topologies — Diego, can you walk the group through the test plan you'll run?
[02:38] Diego Ruiz: Sure. Plan A: controlled lab with three topologies: 1) co-located (Redwood Dedicated single AZ), 2) VPC peered multi-AZ within region, 3) cross-region peered via transit gateway. For each, run 10k requests with a mix of 64/256/512 token prompts. Compare streaming token latencies vs non-streaming full-response, and measure p50/p95/p99 and tail percentiles beyond p99. We'll also capture per-hop traceroute and envoy stats.
[03:05] Ravi Patel: For streaming tests, make sure to simulate real client pacing — our clients sometimes use mobile networks with higher RTT variability.
[03:13] Diego Ruiz: Good call. We'll add a network emulator profile with 20ms +/- 15ms jitter and a mobile profile ~75ms +/- 40ms.
[03:21] Maya Gomez: On KV cache: we deploy an LRU prefix cache on the inference nodes and a distributed KV for long tail prefixes. Can you explain how hot-shard behavior could cause spikes?
[03:32] Diego Ruiz: If a small set of prefixes get high QPS, they may saturate a subset of cache shards. When a shard is evicted or promoted, you'll see a sudden miss that triggers remote fetch and upward latency to the request that hit the miss. That single request then shows up as a p99 spike. There are also locking or serialization points on mutexes around the cache promotion that can cause short blockers.
[03:51] Ethan Brooks: Is there a telemetry signature for those misses?
[03:55] Diego Ruiz: Yes, cache hit ratio per-shard, fetch latency histogram, and thread-block times. We recommend per-shard metrics and tagging by prefix bucket.
[04:05] Clara Li: For streaming, do you buffer tokens at the server side to smooth spikes?
[04:09] Diego Ruiz: Redwood has an optional token-buffering layer — it adds minimal latency (~5-8ms) but reduces jitter by smoothing bursts from our runtime or network. It's a trade-off: small constant latency vs lower tail.
[04:21] Ravi Patel: Hmm, we could accept 5ms extra if it cuts p99 in half.
[04:24] Samira Khan: Important to test both. Also, if you use continuous batching in the runtime, that interacts with streaming in surprising ways. Diego, quick explainer?
[04:33] Diego Ruiz: Continuous batching groups in-flight requests into micro-batches with a short batching window. For streaming, you can drain partial outputs earlier but batching windows can add latency if a request is waiting for a partner. Setting dynamic batch cutoff by token latency and priority can mitigate. If low-latency SLOs are strict, prefer lower batch windows or priority lanes for short prompts.
[04:54] Maya Gomez: We're on a mix of GPUs — some Ampere, some older cards. Could heterogenous GPU pool contribute to tails?
[05:01] Diego Ruiz: Absolutely. If a request lands on a slower GPU or a node with a hot device, you'll see longer runtimes. Smart routing to avoid mixing instance types for latency-critical traffic helps. Redwood supports model variant routing — e.g., route high-SLO traffic to faster quantized fp16 nodes.
[05:17] Ethan Brooks: On-prem fallback — is there a way to run a lightweight local model for failover to avoid cross-region hits?
[05:22] Diego Ruiz: Yes, Redwood Private supports a local lightweight variant pinned for on-prem. It can be a smaller model or more aggressive quantized artifact that maintains acceptable quality with lower latency variance.
[05:34] Clara Li: You mentioned sample E2E runs. What should we provide to make them realistic?
[05:38] Diego Ruiz: Provide 1) representative prompt mix, 2) client RTT distribution, 3) VPC topology and peering config, 4) any envoy/proxy versions. The more accurate, the better diagnostics we'll produce.
[05:48] Ravi Patel: We'll grab traceroutes and envoy stats. Also, we noticed occasional retransmits flagged at the GCP transit gateway logs. Could retransmits cause token gaps?
[05:57] Diego Ruiz: Retransmits add variable delay, yes. Streaming exacerbates that because each token is a new frame. For non-streaming, TCP retransmits may be masked by larger overall transfer.
[06:07] Samira Khan: Let's zoom in on a concrete reproduction. Diego, walk us through a failing trace we shared in the sheet (Row 113).
[06:12] Diego Ruiz: Looking at Row 113 — you see a sudden 420ms jump at hop 4, which corresponds to your transit gateway. After that, tokens show delayed arrivals with bursty inter-token gaps. Also I see a spike in cache miss latency for that request. So it's a compound event: network hop spike plus a cache miss.
[06:32] Maya Gomez: So both together amplify the p99. If either were absent maybe it would stay within SLA.
[06:36] Diego Ruiz: Exactly. Compound failures are common. Our mitigation approach: reduce probability of both happening simultaneously. E.g., 1) replicate hot prefix shards across more nodes, 2) add client-side buffering for streaming, 3) route critical traffic away from peered path during congestion.
[06:51] Ethan Brooks: Replicating shards increases cost — need ROI calculator.
[06:54] Samira Khan: We can provide a cost/perf tradeoff spreadsheet. Diego, note to add cost delta for 2x prefix replication vs buffering.
[07:01] Diego Ruiz: Noted.
[07:03] Clara Li: Any quick wins?
[07:05] Diego Ruiz: Yes — enable per-shard metrics and alert on >2% miss spike, add small token buffering for streaming, and add a routing rule to prefer dedicated low-variance pool for top-traffic routes. Those are low-effort to trial.
[07:18] Ravi Patel: For testing quantization differences, do you recommend int8 or q4_0 style configs?
[07:24] Diego Ruiz: q4_0 or int8 can both reduce latency, but int8 sometimes introduces more scheduling variance on older kernels. q4_0 with per-layer tailoring tends to be more predictable. We'll include quant profiles in the experiment matrix.
[07:36] Maya Gomez: One more thing: our telemetry shows occasional GC pauses in the inference host. How should we identify that vs network?
[07:43] Diego Ruiz: Host-level telemetry: dmesg, iostat, cgroup cpu throttling, and scheduler latency histograms. If the kernel stalled you'll see correlated CPU stalls and syslogs. Network issues will show in tcp retransmit counts and traceroute hop RTT jumps.
[07:57] Samira Khan: Good. We'll capture both sets of telemetry during benchmarks.
[08:01] Diego Ruiz: Final note on SLOs: when customers want p95 and p99 tight, we recommend a multi-tier approach: dedicated low-variance pool for p99-critical traffic + warm prefix caching + small buffering for streaming. Together they reduce the probability of a compound spike.
[08:17] Clara Li: Makes sense. Can you also include an A/B test plan for switching from streaming to non-streaming for a subset of traffic?
[08:23] Diego Ruiz: Yes — we'll propose a canary that routes 5% of traffic to non-streaming and compares 24h p50/p95/p99 and quality metrics.
[08:31] Ethan Brooks: Quality metrics — we need to ensure quantized variant doesn't degrade endpoint accuracy beyond X% BLEU or N/A for our use-case.
[08:38] Diego Ruiz: Understood. We'll include quality regression checks using your sample eval set.
[08:43] Samira Khan: Okay let's recap.
[08:45] Samira Khan: Action items: Diego runs the lab experiments across three topologies and quant profiles; Ravi and Maya share traceroutes and model configs; Redwood to provide cost tradeoff spreadsheet. Follow-up meeting week of 2027-12-13. Any additions?
[08:59] Clara Li: Add in A/B canary for streaming vs non-streaming, and include client RTT emulation for mobile.
[09:06] Diego Ruiz: Added.
[09:08] Ravi Patel: We'll get the logs and traceroutes by Friday.
[09:11] Samira Khan: Great — thanks everyone. We'll send the benchmark plan and calendar invite after.
[09:18] [meeting ends]
